title: Just consent him
topic: Probity in training, research, audit and applications
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a medical ward. The research registrar asks you to take consent from Mr Quinn, 67, for a drug trial, as the research nurse is off sick.

You haven't done Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training, and you aren't on the trial's delegation log.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Offer to do GCP training so you can help in future.
options.brief: Constructive, though it doesn't solve today's problem.
options.detailed: Training would let you support research in future. It ranks third because it doesn't help now.

options.text: Take consent, using the patient information sheet carefully.
options.detailed: However carefully you do it, the consent wouldn't be valid for the trial, and he may not be properly informed.

options.text: Explain to the registrar that you aren't trained or on the delegation log.
options.brief: Only delegated, trained staff can take trial consent.
options.detailed: Trial consent must be taken by people trained and authorised to do it. Explaining this is honest and protects Mr Quinn. It ranks first.

options.text: Tell Mr Quinn that someone from the research team will discuss it with him.
options.detailed: He may be expecting a discussion. Letting him know who will come keeps him informed. It ranks second.

options.text: Take consent, then ask the registrar to sign the form as the consenter.
options.detailed: This misrepresents who took consent, which is dishonest and a serious breach of research governance. It is the least appropriate option.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you recognise the rules on research consent and avoid working outside your authorisation.
explanation.keyDetails: You aren't GCP-trained or on the delegation log. The research nurse is off sick. The registrar is asking you to help.
explanation.reasoning: [C] explains why you can't, [D] keeps the patient informed, and [A] helps in future. [B] works outside your authorisation, and [E] falsifies the record.
explanation.competing: [D] and [A] are close. The key puts the patient first, because he is waiting for a discussion now.
